World History: The Causes of the First World War

Nationalism is an intense loyalty to one's own nation that places national interests above international cooperation. Nationalism differs from militarism in that nationalism concerns collective identity, while militarism concerns the belief that military strength should decide political disputes.

The alliance system divided Europe into two armed camps. The Triple Alliance bound Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy, while the Triple Entente linked France, Russia, and Britain. Because each member promised to defend the others, a local quarrel could pull every great power into a general war.

The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in June 1914 triggered the July Crisis. Austria-Hungary issued an ultimatum to Serbia, and Russia mobilized to protect Serbia. Germany then declared war on Russia and France, so the alliance system converted a Balkan dispute into a continental conflict.

Imperialism increased friction because industrial powers competed for colonies and markets. Competition over Morocco produced two diplomatic crises that hardened the rival blocs.

The Schlieffen Plan was Germany's strategy for avoiding a war on two fronts. The plan required a rapid attack on France through Belgium before Russia could finish mobilizing. When the German advance stalled at the Marne, the plan failed and the war settled into trench warfare.

Trench warfare produced a defensive deadlock. Machine guns and artillery favored defenders, so offensives gained little ground at enormous cost. This stalemate explains why the war lasted four years rather than the few months commanders had predicted.
